verdicts.reasoning: [3] only covers the tribute half. The passage's dominant move (¶3–5, 'It does not work') is the argument that charity is standing in for justice, which [3] leaves out. [1] covers both the tribute and the argument.

¶3 holds everything else equal ('same template,' same disease, same clinic) and pins the gap on 'a man whom fewer people had met.' The passage never credits the niece's skill with the photo, so [0] is unsupported.
The ¶1 sentence states the writer's intent and uncertainty, not a position being argued. The keyed sentence is the actual claim, and ¶5 and ¶6 develop and restate it.

¶5 offers no new evidence about Aurelio. It supplies the charity/justice distinction and mentions 'the Aurelios of the world' only in general terms, so [0] misdescribes ¶5. The key describes both paragraphs accurately.

¶3 is built as a point-by-point match ('the same disease, the same clinic... same template') that isolates one difference, so its method is comparison. There is almost no narration of Aurelio's illness, so [3] misreads the method.
The second clause sharpens the accusation rather than softening it. The semicolon links the rejection of 'generous' to the correction that replaces it, which is what [3] says.

The goal has two parts: invite readers to attend and return to the second-chance idea. Option 2 only reports what happened to Arturo and never invites anyone, so it misses half the goal. The key does both: it names the date ('Bring your transcripts on April 17') and echoes the folded sheet from sentence 7 as 'your own second start.'

Option 0 mentions parents, but it agrees with their preference for prestige and never answers the belief that community college is a lesser choice. The key speaks to parents directly ('your teenager') and pushes back on that belief: the same degree, smaller classes, less debt.

Option 2 is a plain factual report, not a claim anyone could argue with, and it does not preview the later explanation of transfer pathways. The key makes an arguable claim and previews both the anecdote and the concept explained in paragraph 3.

The marathon analogy is about the effort of earning a degree, not about what a transfer agreement guarantees. The key's exchange-rate analogy explains the guarantee itself: students know in advance what their coursework will be worth.

Option 2 keeps the vague, casual wording ('basically,' 'deals,' 'your stuff') that fails the 'clearly' requirement, and it is too loose for a public institution's blog. The key is just as concise and gives a precise definition.

The semicolon correctly joins the two independent clauses without changing the meaning. Option 0 is still a comma splice, option 3 is a splice that also adds a contrast, and option 1 is redundant and adds a cause-and-effect link the original doesn't state.

Option [1] speaks to the worry about having no experience and reassures the reader with a specific fact: crew leaders teach newcomers to use the tools. Option [3] mentions inexperienced people but then says they will probably slow the crew down, which makes the worry worse instead of answering it.

Option [2] gives specific, dated evidence that the trail was actually harmed: a stretch stayed blocked until August, and 'As a result' ties it to the shortfall. Option [3] is a broad guess about what will 'eventually' happen, backed only by 'Everyone knows.' It is not evidence that last year's shortfall did damage.

Option [3] compares forty feet to a hallway classmates walk every day, which helps them picture how short it is. Option [1] compares the lengths of whole trails and has nothing to do with the forty feet.

Option [3] is encouraging and respectful, uses inclusive 'us' and 'our,' and actually urges people to come. Option [0] is respectful, but its stiff, official wording ('is hereby recommended') is neither encouraging nor suited to classmates, and it barely urges anyone.
Option [1] repeats one observation from paragraph 3 and leaves out the breath evidence in sentences 5–6, so it does not sum up how she leads without sound. The key covers both breath and hands.

Option [3] previews only breath and leaves out the hand gestures from paragraph 3, so it fails the requirement to preview two kinds of signals. The key names both breath and hands and makes an arguable claim.
Option [0] agrees with the overstatement instead of qualifying it. The key limits the claim with 'much of' and still sets up the control shown in paragraph 3.

Option [3] claims far more than the evidence shows. The cellist only said players follow the breath 'more closely than' the baton, so 'useless' is unsupported. The key reads the together/ragged contrast correctly as support for the cellist's claim.

In option [0], the misplaced clause 'which happened each time' wrongly attaches to 'the trumpets', which muddles the cause and effect. The key is concise and makes clear that the same result followed each gesture.

The keyed option speaks directly to budget-minded retirees. It compares the cost to a familiar past expense (the hoses) and cuts the garden's share in half. Option 2's claim that the booster would 'pay for itself' is vague and has no support in the passage, since free Wi-Fi brings the garden no money.
The goal has two parts. Option 0 explains why students need the internet but never acknowledges members who finished school without it, so it misses the 'respects members' part. The key does both.
Option 0 is a broad factual generalization, not an arguable claim, and it previews none of the proposal. The key takes a position and names both the booster and the table.
The table is a separate improvement, not an example of the booster, so 'For instance' gets the relationship wrong. 'In addition' signals an added item.

'To address that concern' openly marks sentence 13 as a solution answering the worry. 'Because of that concern' presents the concern as a cause and the students' agreement as its effect. That is a looser fit than labeling the sentence a deliberate response, which is what the stem asks for. The key is the more precise answer.

content.text:
I upheld all five keys. In every case, the passage gives a specific reason the challenged option is wrong.

1. **Key upheld.** In the keyed sentences, the writers grant the board's reasoning ("We understand the logic") and its mandate ("nobody on this board was elected to protect dice"). Then they turn with "But" to dispute the "game" label. Nothing in them claims the volunteers know budgeting better than the board. Mentioning the $140,000 figure only repeats the board's own constraint.

2. **Key upheld.** Paragraph 3 opens with "Consider" right after paragraph 2 contrasts designing a game with playing one. It closes by comparing the game to ecology worksheets. So its main job is to back the design-versus-play claim. The budget comparison comes later, in paragraph 4, which reuses the story as an analogy. That is a secondary use, not the anecdote's main purpose.

3. **Key upheld.** Paragraph 4 works by analogy: "a system of exactly this kind" and "like Dario's village." The costs it names (supervision hours, a crowded homework room, disengagement) are hypothetical costs of where the students would go instead. They are not the district's spending categories. Option 3's description doesn't fit the paragraph.

4. **Key upheld.** "The slower currency of disengagement" is the third item in an "in… in… in" list that follows "the district will pay." The money language makes lost interest one more charge on the bill. Option 3 also calls the opening "brisk," but it is measured and conciliatory.

5. **Key upheld.** "Some" is explicitly partial, and the next sentence ("But the cat game, too, has an economy") keeps the concession in place. So the sentence limits the concession instead of withdrawing it. Nothing suggests that every student builds a complex system.

verdicts.reasoning: The sentences grant the board's reasoning and mandate before the 'But' pivot. Nothing claims the volunteers have more budgeting expertise than the board; the $140,000 figure just restates the board's own constraint.

Paragraph 3 follows directly from paragraph 2's design-versus-play claim ('Consider...') and ends with the comparison to ecology worksheets. Using the story as a budget analogy is a secondary application that comes later, in paragraph 4.

Paragraph 4 works by analogy ('a system of exactly this kind', 'like Dario's village'). The costs it names are hypothetical displacement costs, not a list of the district's spending categories, so option 3 misdescribes the method.

The phrase is the third item in the 'in... in... in' series after 'the district will pay', so it extends the financial diction. The opening paragraph is not 'brisk', and the phrase does not mark a mournful shift.

'Some' is explicitly partial, and the next sentence keeps the concession alive ('the cat game, too, has an economy'). The concession is limited, not withdrawn entirely, and nothing implies that every student builds a complex system.

Paragraph 4 is a deliberate concession, and the clause about 'handing them an excuse' plus 'I would rather the board restore the budget' ties the sentence to funding, which matches [2]. Option [1] is wrong because paragraphs 5 and 6 show the writer is still confident in the swap's value.

The boy hesitates, then comes back and is 'pleased' that someone took the book. That is a visible change in his disposition, and the anecdote makes the point without numbers, as [3] says. Option [0] depends on 'forced,' which the passage contradicts: the book is 'released because somebody decided' to pass it on.

The 'craft not charity' framing appears in paragraph 1 and returns in paragraphs 3 and 6, along with the idea of passing books along, so [3] is the central claim. Option [2] restates paragraph 2, which is background on 'the reason the swap exists,' not the thesis.

Paragraph 4 concedes the swap's limits, and 'And yet' in paragraph 5 introduces a separate benefit. Option [0] puts the claim about giving in paragraph 4, but that claim actually appears in paragraph 5.

Paragraph 2 opens by explaining why the swap exists, and paragraph 3 then turns to what the swap does, which is the structure [3] describes. Option [2] overreads the paragraph: it reports the figures neutrally and never calls the district careless.

'And yet.' is a pivot word that breaks off the list of limits and introduces what the swap uniquely offers. It doesn't summarize anything, and paragraph 5 is not the closing section, since paragraph 6 follows. Option [0] is wrong on both counts.

Option [0] mentions college, but only as a place to keep swimming laps. It says nothing about what kind of community member she wants to be. Option [2] carries the essay's lesson about knowing the regulars and showing up for shared spaces into her future communities.

Option [0] follows the girl's swimming progress, not a connection between strangers. Option [3] says outright that the two did not know each other and shows the bond spreading to her family, which directly supports sentence 5.

Option [2] still says 'nearly everyone' agreed and never presents an opposing view or its reasoning. Option [0] names the dissenters' concern (taxes and road repairs) while keeping her opposition in the main clause, so it meets both parts of the goal.

Option [1] is melodramatic ('a wound upon the very soul of Calder Falls'), which is not a measured tone for admissions readers. Option [0] states her frustration calmly and gives a concrete reason tied to sentence 10.

Option [1] keeps the redundant 'What I learned is that I learned' and drops the 'where decisions are made' idea, so it fails on concision and on meaning. Option [0] is concise and keeps the core lesson, since speaking up where decisions are made implies showing up.
